action.title: Select the end-to-end accumulation ownership family

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: A800 is an Ampere GPU with ample parallelism and native BF16 support, but this kernel has approximately one addition per expert element and cannot exploit tensor cores.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Linear scatter work and native A800 atomics fit the workload substantially better than destination-owned rescanning.

memory_bandwidth.notes: The operation necessarily reads the initial buffer and expert outputs and writes the full result; the demonstrated source-owned family approaches a bandwidth-efficient linear-work implementation.

register_pressure.notes: The proven implementation uses regular 1024-element fragments without materializing duplicate-reduction state.

nodes.notes:
1) Classification: sparse/dynamic gather-scatter reduction. Output is dense [N,3072] BF16, sources are dense [M,3072] BF16, and destination selection is indirect through M int64 indices; N=batch_size*seq_len and M=8N.
2) Canonical math: output[t,h]=final_hidden_states[t,h]+sum_{i:token_indices[i]=t} expert_outputs[i,h]. Hidden coordinates are independent; selected rows contend only when their indices match. Contributions may be reordered subject to BF16 tolerance. Expert outputs are already weighted, so no routing-weight multiply remains.
3) Layout/access: final_hidden_states and expert_outputs are row-major contiguous; token_indices is contiguous but creates random output-row access. Expert values are read once, token indices can be reused across a hidden tile, and destination values undergo atomic RMW. A correct source-owned implementation needs a completed output initialization phase before atomics; there is no grid-wide synchronization within one Triton launch.
4) Regimes: (a) tiny N/M: launch and atomic latency dominate, with limited occupancy; (b) moderate N with random indices: expert streaming plus scattered atomic throughput dominate, and average contention is about eight contributions per destination coordinate; (c) large N/M: memory bandwidth and atomic RMW traffic dominate while random rows weaken cache locality; (d) unusually concentrated indices: serialization/hot-row contention dominates and local aggregation may help.
5) Knobs: source-row versus destination-row ownership, hidden tiling, selected-row grouping, index reuse, duplicate detection scope, BF16 versus wider accumulation, output-copy strategy, warps/stages, masking, and special paths for tiny or highly concentrated workloads.
6) Skeleton: first initialize an independent output from final_hidden_states; then stream selected rows, retain indices and source fragments in registers, and atomically accumulate into output. Destination-owned variants instead initialize and finish each output tile privately, avoiding atomics but requiring discovery of all matching sources. Synchronization is launch-level for copy-then-scatter and block-local only for grouped reduction.
7) Pruned families: source-row scatter accumulation is the general baseline with linear work and atomic contention as limiter; chunk-local duplicate aggregation targets concentrated/small-index regimes but adds comparison and register cost; destination-owned complete accumulation is viable only for tiny domains because scanning or bucketing indices otherwise overwhelms saved atomics.

kernel_summary: This is a BF16 sparse scatter-reduction with dense 3072-wide rows: output[t,h] equals the cloned initial state plus all expert rows whose runtime int64 index selects token t, with M=8N selected rows and arbitrary duplicate destinations. Expert data is contiguous and read once, but output updates are indirect atomic read-modify-writes; thus the general case is expected to be limited by memory/atomic throughput rather than arithmetic on A800, with launch latency important for tiny workloads and hot-row serialization important for concentrated indices. Correctness requires preserving the input, handling arbitrary duplicate indices, and respecting the relatively loose tolerance under nondeterministic BF16 accumulation order.
open_questions: What exact batch_size and seq_len cases are scored, and how much score weight belongs to tiny versus bandwidth-scale workloads?
Does the installed Triton version lower BF16 atomic_add efficiently and correctly on A800, or does it promote, emulate, or reject this atomic type?
Does benchmark timing include output allocation and cloning, and may the implementation use multiple Triton launches inside run()?
Are token_indices always uniformly random as shown, or do any evaluated inputs use structured top-k ordering or unusually concentrated destinations?
What accumulation order and intermediate precision does PyTorch index_add_ use for BF16 on this platform, and how much reordering remains within the stated tolerance?
Are zero-sized dimensions, non-contiguous inputs, aliasing, or hidden sizes other than the declared constant 3072 possible in the evaluator?
